title: Com'era Roccamarina
subtitle: What Roccamarina was like
intro: Dora's photo album on the kitchen table, Pasquale correcting every date, and a town that had one teacher, a port with wooden boats and no asphalt. Then your turn: the snow in Toronto, the Saturday Italian school, nonna's basement kitchen. This unit adds the imperfetto, the tense of how things were and what people used to do, and teaches when to use it and when to use the passato prossimo instead.
objectives: Describe how things were: [[il porto era più piccolo]], [[c'era una sola maestra]], [[non c'era la strada]]
Say what people used to do: [[andavamo a scuola a piedi]], [[mio nonno pescava]], [[giocavo nel cortile]]
Tell background and event together: [[pioveva quando è partito]], [[mentre mangiavamo è arrivata Chiara]]
Talk about childhood: [[da bambino / da bambina]], [[a sei anni]], [[c'era una volta]], [[stavo per…]]
Remember and compare: [[mi ricordo]], [[non mi ricordo]], [[sembrava]], [[è cambiato tutto]]
canDo: A2 · Spoken production: can describe past habits, places and people, and say how things were in the past.
A2 · Spoken interaction: can ask and answer questions about childhood and the past, and compare then and now.
A2 · Listening: can follow a simple description of the past with background and events.
A2 · Writing: can write a short description of childhood or of a place as it used to be.
A2 · Reading: can understand a short memoir-style text with dates and descriptions.

sections.title: L'album di Dora
sections.intro: Dora's album on a rainy Sunday, Pasquale's corrections, and the protagonist's Toronto. Listen for era, c'era, avevamo, andavamo, pescava, and for the passato prossimo breaking in: è partito, ha salutato, è arrivata.

blocks.title: Il porto nel 1962
blocks.setting: Domenica pomeriggio, piove. La cucina di Dora. Un album di fotografie in bianco e nero, un caffè, Pasquale sulla sedia buona.

lines.t: Guarda. Questo è il porto nel 1962. Le barche erano di legno e i pescatori uscivano alle quattro di mattina.
lines.n: Look. This is the port in 1962. The boats were wooden and the fishermen went out at four in the morning.
lines.note: Erano, uscivano: the imperfetto. How things were, what people used to do.

lines.t: Alle tre. Mio padre usciva alle tre.
lines.n: At three. My father went out at three.
lines.note: Usciva: he used to go out. Pasquale corrects everything. Get used to it.

lines.t: Alle tre, alle quattro. Non c'era la strada asfaltata, c'era la terra. E qui, questa è la scuola. C'era una sola maestra per tutti: la maestra Carmela.
lines.n: Three, four. There was no asphalt road, there was dirt. And here, this is the school. There was only one teacher for everybody: Miss Carmela.
lines.note: C'era, non c'era: there was, there wasn't. The imperfetto of c'è.

lines.t: Una maestra sola? Per quanti bambini?
lines.n: Only one teacher? For how many children?

lines.t: Quaranta. Dalla prima alla quinta nella stessa stanza. Io ero il più bravo.
lines.n: Forty. From first to fifth grade in the same room. I was the best.
lines.note: Ero: I was. Pasquale's favourite sentence.

lines.t: Tu eri il più antipatico. Correggevi anche la maestra.
lines.n: You were the most unpleasant. You even corrected the teacher.
lines.note: Eri, correggevi: you were, you used to correct. Sixty years later, nothing has changed.

lines.t: Andavamo a scuola a piedi, anche con la pioggia. Non avevamo il grembiule nero, avevamo quello bianco. E il pomeriggio aiutavamo in campagna: mia madre raccoglieva le olive e io portavo l'acqua.
lines.n: We walked to school, even in the rain. We didn't have the black smock, we had the white one. And in the afternoon we helped in the fields: my mother picked olives and I carried the water.
lines.note: Andavamo, avevamo, aiutavamo, raccoglieva, portavo: five habits in the imperfetto.

lines.t: E questa? Chi sono?
lines.n: And this one? Who are they?

lines.t: Questa è la stazione. Il 12 aprile 1969. Il giorno che tuo nonno Cosimo è partito. Pioveva, e tutto il paese era lì.
lines.n: This is the station. 12 April 1969. The day your grandfather Cosimo left. It was raining, and the whole town was there.
lines.note: È partito: the event, passato prossimo. Pioveva, era: the background, imperfetto. The whole unit in one line.

lines.t: Non pioveva. C'era il sole. Tu avevi undici anni e piangevi. Io ne avevo quindici e ho portato la valigia.
lines.n: It wasn't raining. It was sunny. You were eleven and you were crying. I was fifteen and I carried the suitcase.
lines.note: Avevi undici anni: age in the imperfetto. Ho portato la valigia: one action, passato prossimo.

lines.t: Pioveva. Lo so perché avevo le scarpe nuove e si sono rovinate.
lines.n: It was raining. I know because I had new shoes and they got ruined.
lines.note: Avevo: a state. Si sono rovinate: what happened to them.

lines.t: Va bene, pioveva. Cosimo ha salutato tutti, è salito sul treno e non ha detto niente. Suo figlio, tuo padre, aveva sei anni e dormiva.
lines.n: All right, it was raining. Cosimo said goodbye to everyone, got on the train and said nothing. His son, your father, was six and was sleeping.
lines.note: Ha salutato, è salito, non ha detto: three events. Aveva, dormiva: two descriptions.

lines.t: Mio padre non ricorda niente del viaggio. Nonno non ne parlava mai.
lines.n: My father doesn't remember anything of the journey. Grandpa never used to talk about it.
lines.note: Non ne parlava mai: he never used to talk about it. Ne = about it, unit 14.

lines.t: Nessuno ne parlava. Si partiva e basta. Adesso parliamo tutti, e non parte nessuno.
lines.n: Nobody talked about it. You left and that was it. Now we all talk, and nobody leaves.
lines.note: Si partiva: people left, impersonal si with the imperfetto. Adesso parliamo: the present, for the contrast.

notes.phrase: era · c'era · erano · avevo · avevi · andavamo · usciva
notes.note: The imperfetto: regular endings on almost every verb (-avo, -evo, -ivo), and essere as ero, eri, era, eravamo, eravate, erano.

notes.phrase: Pioveva, e tuo nonno è partito.
notes.note: Background in the imperfetto, event in the passato prossimo. Ask: is this the scenery or the action? Scenery: imperfetto. Action: passato prossimo.

notes.phrase: Tu avevi undici anni. · Io ne avevo quindici.
notes.note: Age in the past is always the imperfetto. Ne avevo quindici = I was fifteen (of them).

notes.phrase: Non ne parlava mai. · Si partiva e basta.
notes.note: Habits that lasted: imperfetto. E basta = and that was that.

blocks.title: Da bambino a Toronto
blocks.setting: Più tardi, la stessa cucina. Chiara è arrivata con i pasticciotti. L'album è chiuso; le domande no.

lines.t: E tu? Com'era Toronto quando eri {{piccolo|piccola}}?
lines.n: And you? What was Toronto like when you were little?
lines.note: Com'era…? What was it like? Quando eri piccolo / piccola: when you were little.

t.m: Fredda. Da bambino aspettavo la neve da ottobre. La prima neve arrivava a novembre e restava fino ad aprile. Andavamo a scuola con gli stivali e portavamo le scarpe nello zaino.
t.f: Fredda. Da bambina aspettavo la neve da ottobre. La prima neve arrivava a novembre e restava fino ad aprile. Andavamo a scuola con gli stivali e portavamo le scarpe nello zaino.
t.note: Da bambino / da bambina: as a child. The one word that changes with the protagonist. Aspettavo, arrivava, restava, andavamo, portavamo: habits.

lines.n: Cold. As a child I waited for the snow from October. The first snow came in November and stayed until April. We went to school in boots and carried our shoes in our backpacks.

lines.t: E l'italiano? Dove l'hai imparato? Parli bene, per {{un canadese|una canadese}}.
lines.n: And Italian? Where did you learn it? You speak well, for a Canadian.
lines.note: Dove l'hai imparato? One question about a finished fact: passato prossimo. L' = lo = l'italiano.

lines.t: Il sabato mattina andavo alla scuola italiana, in una chiesa su St. Clair. Mentre i miei amici dormivano, io imparavo i verbi. Lo odiavo.
lines.n: On Saturday mornings I went to Italian school, in a church on St. Clair. While my friends were sleeping, I was learning verbs. I hated it.
lines.note: Mentre i miei amici dormivano, io imparavo: two things going on together, both imperfetto. Odiavo: a state.

lines.t: E adesso li correggi tu, i verbi.
lines.n: And now you're the one correcting the verbs.
lines.note: Li correggi tu: you correct them, with tu at the end for emphasis.

lines.t: E poi c'era la cucina di nonna, nel seminterrato. Una cucina intera sotto casa: il sugo la domenica, le conserve a settembre, i pomodori in cantina. Nonno raccontava storie di Roccamarina mentre nonna faceva le orecchiette. Io non ascoltavo. Stavo per chiedergli della casa, un giorno, e poi non gliel'ho mai chiesto.
lines.n: And then there was nonna's kitchen, in the basement. A whole kitchen under the house: sauce on Sundays, preserves in September, tomatoes in the cellar. Grandpa told stories about Roccamarina while nonna made orecchiette. I didn't listen. I was about to ask him about the house, one day, and then I never asked him.
lines.note: C'era, raccontava, faceva, ascoltavo: description. Stavo per chiedergli: I was about to ask him. Non gliel'ho mai chiesto: the event that didn't happen, passato prossimo.

lines.t: Una cucina nel seminterrato? Perché?
lines.n: A kitchen in the basement? Why?

lines.t: Perché quella di sopra era bella e non si usava. Tutti gli italiani di Toronto avevano due cucine: una per guardare e una per cucinare.
lines.n: Because the one upstairs was nice and wasn't used. All the Italians in Toronto had two kitchens: one to look at and one to cook in.
lines.note: Era, non si usava, avevano: three imperfetti. The truest sentence about Italian Canada.

lines.t: Qui ne avevamo una, e si usava.
lines.n: Here we had one, and it was used.
lines.note: Ne avevamo una: we had one (of them).

lines.t: E tuo nonno, com'era?
lines.n: And your grandfather, what was he like?

lines.t: Alto, silenzioso. Sembrava severo, ma non lo era. Mi ricordo le mani: grandi, con la calce sotto le unghie anche la domenica. Non si lamentava mai. Diceva solo: lavora.
lines.n: Tall, quiet. He seemed strict, but he wasn't. I remember his hands: big, with lime under the nails even on Sundays. He never complained. He only said: work.
lines.note: Sembrava, era, si lamentava, diceva: character and habits. Mi ricordo: I remember.

lines.t: Diceva «fatìa». In dialetto. Lavoro si dice fatìa, qui.
lines.n: He said «fatìa». In dialect. Work is called fatìa, here.
lines.note: Pasquale corrects the Italian into dialect, for once. See Living there.

lines.t: E stava per dirlo anche a te, quando è morto il pomeriggio. Dai, mangia un pasticciotto. Sei troppo {{magro|magra}}.
lines.n: And he was about to say it to you too, when the afternoon died. Come on, eat a pasticciotto. You're too thin.
lines.note: Stava per dirlo: was about to say it. Dora changes the subject the Italian way: with food.

notes.phrase: da bambino / da bambina · quando ero piccolo / piccola · a sei anni
notes.note: Three ways to say "as a child". The first two change with the protagonist.

notes.phrase: Mentre i miei amici dormivano, io imparavo i verbi.
notes.note: Mentre + imperfetto: two actions in parallel. Quando + passato prossimo: an event that interrupts.

notes.phrase: Stavo per chiedergli… e non gliel'ho mai chiesto.
notes.note: Stare per + infinitive = to be about to. In the imperfetto: was about to.

notes.phrase: Sembrava severo, ma non lo era.
notes.note: Sembrare: to seem. Lo = it (strict), standing for the adjective.

questions.q: Dora and Pasquale agree that it was raining when Cosimo left.
questions.t: Non pioveva. C'era il sole. — Pioveva.
questions.why: Pasquale says it was sunny; Dora says it was raining because her new shoes got ruined. Pasquale gives in.

questions.q: Why did the Italians of Toronto have two kitchens?
options: One to look at, one to cook in.
One for the summer, one for the winter.
One for the grandparents, one for the children.
questions.why: Una per guardare e una per cucinare: the upstairs kitchen was nice and wasn't used.

questions.q: Da {{bambino|bambina}} ___ (io, aspettare) la neve da ottobre. Il sabato ___ (andare) alla scuola italiana mentre i miei amici ___ (dormire).
questions.n: As a child I waited for the snow from October. On Saturdays I went to Italian school while my friends slept.

sections.title: Infanzia, scuola, mare, memoria
sections.intro: The words of childhood and school, the old objects and jobs of the town, the sea and the port, and the verbs of remembering.

items.n: childhood

ex.t: Ho passato l'infanzia a Toronto.
ex.n: I spent my childhood in Toronto.

items.note: Da bambino / da bambina is what people say; l'infanzia is the noun. Scuola dell'infanzia: nursery school.

items.n: child, little boy

ex.t: Quaranta bambini e una maestra.
ex.n: Forty children and one teacher.

items.note: Bambino up to about ten; then ragazzo / ragazza. Da bambino: as a child.

items.n: to play

ex.t: Giocavamo nel cortile fino a sera.
ex.n: We played in the courtyard until evening.

items.note: Giocare a + game / sport: giocare a calcio, a nascondino, a carte. Suonare for instruments.

items.n: game, toy

ex.t: Non avevamo giochi: avevamo la strada.
ex.n: We didn't have toys: we had the street.

items.note: Giocattolo: toy (the object). Gioco: game, play.

items.n: ball (football)

ex.t: Un pallone per tutto il paese.
ex.n: One ball for the whole town.

items.note: Palla: a small ball. Giocare a pallone: to play football, in the street.

items.n: hide-and-seek

ex.t: Giocavamo a nascondino tra le barche.
ex.n: We played hide-and-seek among the boats.

items.note: From nascondere, to hide. Acchiapparello: tag.

items.n: courtyard, yard

ex.t: Il cortile della scuola era di terra.
ex.n: The school yard was dirt.

items.note: Every Italian school and building has one. Giardino: garden.

items.n: primary school teacher

ex.t: La maestra Carmela insegnava a quaranta bambini.
ex.n: Miss Carmela taught forty children.

items.note: Maestro / maestra for primary school; professore / professoressa from middle school on. Also maestro = master (of music, of a craft).

items.n: smock, apron

ex.t: A scuola portavamo il grembiule bianco con il fiocco.
ex.n: At school we wore a white smock with a bow.

items.note: Italian primary children still wear one in many schools: blue or black for boys, white for girls, or one colour for all.

items.n: school bag

ex.t: La cartella era di cartone e pesava poco.
ex.n: The school bag was cardboard and weighed little.

items.note: Also a folder and a computer folder. Zaino: backpack, what children carry now.

items.n: homework

ex.t: Facevo i compiti sul tavolo della cucina.
ex.n: I did my homework on the kitchen table.

items.note: Always plural. Fare i compiti. Un compito in classe: a test.

items.n: blackboard

ex.t: Una lavagna nera e un pezzo di gesso.
ex.n: A black blackboard and a piece of chalk.

items.note: Gesso: chalk. Lavagna from the slate of Lavagna, a town in Liguria.

items.n: once, in the old days

ex.t: Una volta qui non c'era niente. C'era una volta…
ex.n: In the old days there was nothing here. Once upon a time…

items.note: Una volta + imperfetto = used to. C'era una volta: once upon a time, the start of every fairy tale.

items.n: then, at that time; so

ex.t: Allora non c'era la strada. Allora, cosa facciamo?
ex.n: Back then there was no road. So, what do we do?

items.note: Two meanings: at that time (with the imperfetto) and so / well (to start a sentence).

items.n: in those days

ex.t: A quei tempi si partiva e basta.
ex.n: In those days you left and that was it.

items.note: Also all'epoca, ai miei tempi (in my day), a quell'epoca.

items.n: farmer, peasant

ex.t: I nonni di Dora erano contadini.
ex.n: Dora's grandparents were farmers.

items.note: Campagna: the countryside and the fields. In campagna: in the fields.

items.n: fisherman

ex.t: I pescatori uscivano alle tre e tornavano a mezzogiorno.
ex.n: The fishermen went out at three and came back at noon.

items.note: Pescare: to fish. Pesce: fish. Pesca: fishing (and peach).

items.n: boat

ex.t: Le barche erano di legno e si dipingevano ogni primavera.
ex.n: The boats were wooden and were painted every spring.

items.note: Barca a vela: sailing boat. Nave: ship. Gozzo: the traditional fishing boat of the south.

items.n: net; network

ex.t: Le donne riparavano le reti sul molo.
ex.n: The women mended the nets on the pier.

items.note: Also the network and the internet: la rete. And the goal in football.

items.n: pier, jetty

ex.t: Il molo era più corto e di pietra.
ex.n: The pier was shorter and made of stone.

items.note: Banchina: the quay. Porto: the harbour.

items.n: well

ex.t: L'acqua si prendeva dal pozzo in piazza.
ex.n: Water was taken from the well in the square.

items.note: Running water came to many southern villages only in the 1960s.

items.n: donkey

ex.t: Mio nonno andava in campagna con l'asino.
ex.n: My grandfather went to the fields with the donkey.

items.note: Also "dunce": sei un asino. Carretto: cart.

items.n: television

ex.t: C'era una sola televisione, al bar, in bianco e nero.
ex.n: There was only one television, at the bar, in black and white.

items.note: Il televisore: the set. La TV (tivù). In bianco e nero: black and white.

items.n: suitcase

ex.t: La valigia di cartone: il simbolo dell'emigrazione.
ex.n: The cardboard suitcase: the symbol of emigration.

items.note: Fare la valigia: to pack. Plural valigie (or valige).

items.n: to remember; to remind

ex.t: Ricordo le mani di mio nonno. Mi ricordo di quel giorno.
ex.n: I remember my grandfather's hands. I remember that day.

items.note: Ricordare + object, or ricordarsi di + object: same meaning. Ricordare a qualcuno di: to remind someone to.

items.n: to forget

ex.t: Ho dimenticato il nome della maestra. Non dimenticarti di chiamare.
ex.n: I've forgotten the teacher's name. Don't forget to call.

items.note: Dimenticare or dimenticarsi di. Scordare: same, more colloquial.

items.n: to seem, to look like

ex.t: Sembrava severo, ma non lo era. Sembra ieri.
ex.n: He seemed strict, but he wasn't. It seems like yesterday.

items.note: Mi sembra che…: it seems to me that. Sembra + adjective, sembra di + infinitive.

items.n: to change

ex.t: È cambiato tutto. Il paese è cambiato, Pasquale no.
ex.n: Everything has changed. The town has changed, Pasquale hasn't.

items.note: Essere when something changes by itself (è cambiato); avere when you change something (ho cambiato casa).

items.n: to imagine

ex.t: Non immaginavo un paese così piccolo.
ex.n: I didn't imagine such a small town.

items.note: Immagino! = I can imagine! Immaginarsi: to picture oneself.

items.n: to tell (a story), to recount

ex.t: Nonno raccontava storie di Roccamarina.
ex.n: Grandpa used to tell stories about Roccamarina.

items.note: Raccontare a story; dire a thing. Un racconto: a short story.

items.n: to grow up, to grow

ex.t: Sono cresciuto a Toronto. I bambini crescono in fretta.
ex.n: I grew up in Toronto. Children grow up fast.

items.note: Essere, participle cresciuto. Also to raise: ha cresciuto tre figli (avere).

items.n: strict

ex.t: La maestra era severa ma giusta.
ex.n: The teacher was strict but fair.

items.note: Not "severe" in the medical sense: that is grave.

items.n: quiet, silent

ex.t: Nonno era alto e silenzioso.
ex.n: Grandpa was tall and quiet.

items.note: Tranquillo: calm. Zitto: silent (stai zitto = be quiet).

items.n: to be about to

ex.t: Stavo per chiederglielo. Sta per piovere.
ex.n: I was about to ask him. It's about to rain.

items.note: Stare per + infinitive. Present: sto per; past: stavo per.

sections.title: Era, c'era, andavamo: the imperfetto
sections.intro: Five pieces: the forms of the imperfetto, its uses, the choice between imperfetto and passato prossimo, the expressions of childhood with stare per, and the verbs of memory. Reference pages at the end of each block.

blocks.title: Imperfetto: the forms
blocks.rule: Take the infinitive, drop -re, add -vo, -vi, -va, -vamo, -vate, -vano: parlavo, prendevo, dormivo. Every verb follows this except essere (ero, eri, era, eravamo, eravate, erano) and a handful that use an old stem: fare → facevo, dire → dicevo, bere → bevevo, tradurre → traducevo, porre → ponevo, trarre → traevo. The stress falls on the stem in io, tu, lui and loro (parLAvo, parLAvano) and on the ending in noi and voi (parlaVAmo).

blocks.caption: [[parlare|to speak]], [[avere|to have]], [[essere|to be]] · imperfetto
blocks.note: Avere is regular (avevo). Essere is the only truly irregular one: ero, eri, era, eravamo, eravate, erano.

blocks.caption: The old-stem verbs
head: Infinitive
Stem
io
noi
loro
blocks.note: Compounds follow: rifare → rifacevo, produrre → producevo, proporre → proponevo. C'è → c'era, ci sono → c'erano.

items.t: Le barche erano di legno e i pescatori uscivano alle tre.
items.n: The boats were wooden and the fishermen went out at three.

items.t: Avevo undici anni, andavo a scuola a piedi e facevo i compiti in cucina.
items.n: I was eleven, I walked to school and did my homework in the kitchen.

items.t: C'era una sola maestra. Non c'erano macchine. Si beveva l'acqua del pozzo.
items.n: There was only one teacher. There were no cars. People drank water from the well.

items.t: Nonno diceva poco e faceva molto.
items.n: Grandpa said little and did a lot.

items.wrong: io parlavo → io parlava; loro parlavano → loro parlavo
fare → favo; dire → divo; bere → bevo (that's the present)
essere → essevo · era → ero (for lui)
parlaVAno (stress on va)
items.why: Loro is stressed on the stem, like the present.

blocks.title: What the imperfetto is for
blocks.rule: The imperfetto paints the past without saying when it started or ended: habits and repeated actions (andavo a scuola a piedi), descriptions of people, places and things (il porto era piccolo), age, time, weather and dates (avevo sei anni, erano le tre, pioveva), states of mind (volevo, sapevo, pensavo), and an action in progress as background (dormiva quando…). English: used to, would, was doing, or a plain simple past.

head: Use
Italian
English
rows: Andavamo a scuola a piedi. Mio padre usciva alle tre.
We used to walk to school. My father would go out at three.
Il porto era piccolo. Le barche erano di legno. Nonno era alto.
The port was small. The boats were wooden. Grandpa was tall.
Avevo undici anni. Tuo padre aveva sei anni.
I was eleven. Your father was six.
Erano le tre. Era il 12 aprile. Pioveva. C'era il sole.
It was three o'clock. It was 12 April. It was raining. It was sunny.
Volevo restare. Non sapevo niente. Pensavo di tornare.
I wanted to stay. I didn't know anything. I thought I'd come back.
Dormiva quando il treno è partito.
He was sleeping when the train left.
While nonna cooked, grandpa told stories.
Volevo un caffè. Cercavo un locale.
I'd like a coffee. I'm looking for premises.

items.t: Da bambino aspettavo la neve. Arrivava a novembre e restava fino ad aprile.
items.n: As a child I waited for the snow. It came in November and stayed until April.

items.t: Era il 1969, avevo quindici anni e il paese non aveva ancora la strada.
items.n: It was 1969, I was fifteen and the town still didn't have the road.

items.t: Volevo chiedergli della casa, ma non sapevo come.
items.n: I wanted to ask him about the house, but I didn't know how.

items.t: Buongiorno, volevo un etto di prosciutto.
items.n: Good morning, I'd like a hundred grams of ham.
items.note: the polite imperfetto: present meaning, softer than voglio

blocks.title: Used to, would, was doing
blocks.text: English spreads the imperfetto over three or four forms. [[Andavo a scuola a piedi]] is *I used to walk*, *I would walk* or just *I walked*. [[Dormiva]] is *he was sleeping* or *he slept*. [[Era alto]] is *he was tall*, full stop. The Italian question is simpler than the English one: is this the background, the way things were? Then imperfetto.

items.wrong: Ho avuto undici anni nel 1969.
Ieri ha piovuto tutto il giorno. (fine) → Pioveva quando è partito → Ha piovuto quando è partito.
Sono andato a scuola a piedi ogni giorno. (for a habit)

blocks.title: Imperfetto or passato prossimo?
blocks.rule: Passato prossimo for events: things that happened once, started and finished, moved the story on (è partito, ho portato la valigia, si sono rovinate). Imperfetto for the frame around them: how things were, what was going on, what used to happen (pioveva, aveva sei anni, dormiva). Mentre introduces a background action (mentre dormiva…); quando usually introduces the event (quando è partito…). Some verbs change meaning: sapevo (I knew) vs ho saputo (I found out); conoscevo (I knew) vs ho conosciuto (I met); volevo (I wanted) vs ho voluto (I insisted); potevo (I could) vs ho potuto (I managed).

blocks.text: Imagine the story as a film. What the camera shows while nothing happens, the set, the weather, the faces, the habits, is the imperfetto. What makes the next shot different, the door that opens, the train that leaves, the sentence someone says, is the passato prossimo. [[Pioveva]] (camera on the rain) [[e tuo nonno è partito]] (cut to the train).

blocks.title: da bambino, c'era una volta, stare per
blocks.rule: Da + noun for a stage of life: da bambino / da bambina, da ragazzo, da giovane, da grande (when I grow up), da vecchio. A + age: a sei anni. C'era una volta opens a tale; una volta + imperfetto = once / in the old days. Stare per + infinitive = to be about to; in the imperfetto, stavo per = I was about to (and usually didn't, or was interrupted). Stare + gerund in the imperfetto: stavo mangiando = I was (in the middle of) eating.

sections.title: L'amico, un'amica, un bel giorno: elision and truncation
sections.intro: Spoken Italian runs words together. Two things make it sound natural: elision (dropping a final vowel before another vowel: l'amico, un'amica, dov'è, c'era) and truncation (dropping a final vowel or syllable before a consonant: un bel giorno, buon lavoro, signor Russo, San Rocco). One takes an apostrophe, the other does not.

blocks.caption: Elision: before a vowel, with an apostrophe
head: Full
Elided
English
rows: dove è · come è · che è
where is · how is · that is
lo ho visto · la ho vista
I saw him · I saw her
blocks.note: Un (masculine) never takes an apostrophe: un amico. Un'amica, with the apostrophe, is feminine. This is the most common spelling mistake Italians make.

blocks.caption: Truncation: before a consonant, no apostrophe
head: Full
Truncated
English
rows: signore Russo · dottore Moro · professore Leone
signor Russo · dottor Moro · professor Leone
Mr Russo · Dr Moro · Professor Leone
ben fatto · mal di testa · fin qui
well done · headache · up to here
blocks.note: Qual è is the famous one: no apostrophe, because qual is a truncation, not an elision. Italians argue about it; the dictionaries don't.

pairs.nb: how it sounds: one stream, no gaps
pairs.tip: Vowels link across the word boundaries: c'era‿una‿volta.
The apostrophe is silent; the words run together.

blocks.title: Reading aloud
blocks.text: When you read Italian aloud, do not pause at the apostrophe or between a word that ends in a vowel and one that starts with a vowel: [[c'era‿una‿volta‿un paese]]. Italian has almost no glottal stops, the little catch English puts before a vowel. Run the vowels into each other and you will sound ten times more fluent with no new grammar.

sections.title: Il Sud degli anni Sessanta, la scuola, il dialetto
sections.intro: The cardboard suitcase, the school system then and now, the Saturday Italian schools of Toronto, and what Dora speaks when Pasquale isn't listening.

blocks.text: In the 1960s southern Italy was still largely rural and poor while the North was living its [[boom economico]]. From Puglia, Calabria, Sicily and Campania, millions left: to Turin and Milan for the factories, on the [[Treno del Sole]] from Palermo and Lecce; to Germany and Switzerland as [[Gastarbeiter]]; to Canada, Australia, Argentina and the United States by ship. The [[valigia di cartone]], the cardboard suitcase tied with string, is the image of that departure and the title of a hundred songs and books. Running water, asphalt, electricity in every house and a school in every village arrived in the South in the same years the people were leaving. By 1975 Roccamarina had lost a third of its population and gained its first television in the bar, its first tractor and its first tourists. Dora's album is the record of the ten years in which everything changed.

In 1962 Italy made the [[scuola media]] compulsory up to fourteen; before that, village children stopped at the fifth year of [[elementari]], often with a single teacher for all classes ([[pluriclasse]]), as in Dora's school. Today the system is: [[asilo nido]] (0 to 3), [[scuola dell'infanzia]] (3 to 6), [[scuola primaria]] (6 to 11, five years, with the famous smocks), [[scuola secondaria di primo grado]] (11 to 14, still called le medie), then five years of [[scuola secondaria di secondo grado]]: a [[liceo]] (classico, scientifico, linguistico, artistico…), an [[istituto tecnico]] or an [[istituto professionale]], ending at nineteen with the [[maturità]], the state exam. University is three years plus two. School is six days a week in many places, mornings only, with afternoons for homework and the [[oratorio]] or the street.

blocks.title: La scuola del sabato a Toronto
blocks.text: From the 1960s, the Italian communities of Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver organised [[scuole del sabato]]: Saturday morning classes in church halls and school basements, run by parishes, the [[Dante Alighieri Society]], and later funded by the Italian consulates and by Ontario's heritage-language programme. Thousands of Italo-Canadian children spent their Saturdays conjugating verbs while their friends watched cartoons. Most hated it; many are grateful now. The protagonist's Italian, and the accent Pasquale calls «a Canadian's», come from there and from a basement kitchen.

Dora speaks Italian to you and [[salentino]] to Pasquale, to Nando and to her tomatoes. Salentino is not bad Italian: it is a dialect of the Sicilian group, with its own grammar ([[fatìa]] for lavoro, [[sciamu]] for andiamo, [[lu mare]] for il mare), older than standard Italian and the first language of everyone over sixty in Roccamarina. Standard Italian, based on literary Tuscan, became the spoken language of the whole country only after 1954, through television ([[Non è mai troppo tardi]], the TV school that taught adults to read), through compulsory school, and through the migrations that mixed everyone in Turin and Toronto. Pasquale, the retired teacher, is the voice of that standard: he corrects Dora's dialect, your participles and the mayor's subjunctives. Dora is the voice of the place. You need both: Italian to be understood everywhere, and enough dialect to understand what Dora says when she is angry.

blocks.title: What to do with dialect
blocks.text: Learn to recognise it, not to speak it. A few words ([[fatìa]], [[sciamu]], [[bbona]]) said with a smile earn you affection; a whole sentence from a foreigner sounds like a joke. When someone switches to dialect, ask [[come si dice in italiano?]]: it is a compliment to their language, and they will translate with pleasure, and at length.
